title: Copland, the Popular Front, and why Jang writes programmatic works
summary: Jang describes his commission for the 1911 revolution centennial, Copland's Lincoln Portrait, the Popular Front and accessible music.

blocks.x: progressives, social democrats, liberals, Roosevelt-new dealers — it was a kind of a united front or a coalition. And of course you know about, because of that movement, you know Roosevelt created the Works Progress Administration, which provided work for artists, you know, and sometimes labor union contexts. And Aaron Copland wanted to — one of his musical goals was that we need to change the music so that it would become more accessible to the public. Because the public was alienated by sort of the you know, the Schoenberg’s utilization. And so that was one reason why, you know, I write these works that have programmatic titles. The other reason is that we forget about history, and these important great artists such as Paul Robeson, or, you know, a great leader of modern China, Sun Yat-sen. And also, the relationship of Sun Yat-sen was inspired by Lincoln. They both wanted to unify their countries by building the railroad. Lincoln through the Railroad Act of 1862. He never saw it realized. It was completed by Chinese immigrants in 1869. He could envision it. Because he died before that. Or Sun Yat-sen, he was ahead of his time. I guess China was not unified. It was dominated by foreign imperialists, you know, the Ching dynasty — a large country with bandits and so forth — it was undeveloped. So that’s partly why at this point in my life, you know, where legacy is very important —
